chunks.content: Introduction Stroke encompasses a group of acute cerebral circulatory disorders stemming from limited or comprehensive cerebral impairment syndrome, including two categories: ischemic stroke and hemorrhagic stroke. This condition is characterized by high morbidity, high disability, high mortality, high recurrence rates, and a significant economic burden, all of which severely impact patients’ health status and quality of life [ – ]. According to some data [ , ], 70% to 80% of stroke survivors experience varying degrees of functional limb movement disorders, which severely limit their daily abilities and impose a heavy burden on their families and society. Several studies have concluded that hemiplegia, as the primary limb dysfunction, does not stem from the destruction of the motor system itself. Instead, it results from the acute neurological dysfunction caused by the disease, also known as disuse disorder. Moreover, the brain’s neurons exhibit plasticity after a stroke, making early rehabilitation training an effective means of promoting the recovery of patients’ neurological functions, thereby reducing disability and enhancing the quality of life [ , ]. The survey found that the level of exercise rehabilitation for stroke patients was far below the guideline recommendations [ ]. As the disease progressed, patients gradually exhibited the “three lows” of lack of initiative, weakened adherence, and reduced willingness to participate. Therefore, an in-depth understanding of the actual experiences and needs of stroke patients during physical rehabilitation is of great significance for optimizing rehabilitation strategies and enhancing rehabilitation outcomes. However, employing a single qualitative research method makes it challenging to comprehensively reflect on the genuine experiences of exercise rehabilitation for stroke patients and their real-life dilemmas in the participation process due to limitations in the representativeness of the sample group, the interview process design, and potential subjective biases present during the interviews. Previous systematic reviews and meta-synthesis have explored related research questions. For example, one systematic review examined the experiences of stroke patients during physical rehabilitation [ ], but the included studies were all published before 2015. The incidence of stroke has been rising in recent years, as has the number of studies investigating patients’ experiences with rehabilitation. Furthermore, as society evolves and patients’ rehabilitation strategies may shift—from traditional methods to those based on handheld games, virtual reality, or rehabilitation robots—their experiences and needs during physical rehabilitation may also differ. Another systematic review examined the rehabilitation needs of patients after departing from medical institutions [ ]. But the study did not concentrate on physical rehabilitation and lacked insights into patients’ experiences during hospitalization and rehabilitation in specialized facilities. Patients typically opt for treatment in a professional institution during the acute or subacute stages, and only when their condition is relatively stable do they choose to leave the medical institution in favor of home or community rehabilitation. However, the feelings and needs of patients vary across different illness stages and settings. Given this, the present study conducted another systematic assessment and meta-synthesis of studies related to the real experiences and needs of stroke patients in physical rehabilitation. It aims to dig deeper into their inner feelings, practical needs, and real barriers in the process of exercise rehabilitation, and to address the shortcomings of previous reviews in terms of timeliness, specificity to physical rehabilitation, and inclusion of technology-mediated interventions. In order to provide a scientific basis of reference framework for the subsequent development of targeted strategies to promote exercise rehabilitation and optimise practice pathways for stroke patients. The review Aim This study aims to systematically evaluate and integrate the real experiences and unmet needs of stroke patients in the process of physical rehabilitation, to reveal the patients’ inner feelings, practical barriers, and core demands when participating in exercise rehabilitation, to provide a scientific basis for optimizing personalized and patient-centered rehabilitation intervention strategies, and ultimately to enhance rehabilitation adherence and long-term rehabilitation outcomes. Methods This study follows the Enhancing Transparency in Reporting Qualitative Research Reviews (ENTREQ) [ ] and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) [ ], to ensure transparency in research reporting (Supplementary Material 1). The program was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024594929). Using the three-step search strategy recommended by Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI), an initial limited search was conducted on PubMed and CNKI, followed by an analysis of the words contained in the title and abstract and the index terms used to describe the article. A second search was then conducted in all selected databases using the identified keywords and relevant indexing terms. Finally, a complete retrospective search of the bibliographies of all references selected for inclusion in the literature was performed, and a search of Google Scholar for unpublished reports and related articles was performed. The complete search strategy is described in Supplementary Material 2. Eligibility criteria The PICoS (Population, Phenomenon of Interest, Context, Study design) model recommended by JBI was used to develop the screening criteria for this study. Inclusion criteria were as follows: P (population) was stroke patients ≥ 18 years of age with residual limb dysfunction who had received rehabilitation for limb function, and excluded stroke patients with preexisting limb dysfunction before stroke or limb dysfunction that occurred after stroke but was not caused by stroke.; I (phenomenal interest) was the experiences, feelings, or needs of the physical rehabilitation process; Co (context) was any setting (e.g., home, hospital, community, rehabilitation facility, etc.), and cultural context, and in any geographic location; and S (study design) was a qualitative study, including phenomenological research, grounded theory, ethnography, and other qualitative research methods. Exclusion criteria were as follows: articles not in English or Chinese, reviews, conference abstracts, qualitative research data that could not be extracted from mixed-methods approaches, and articles for which the full text was not available. Study selection The results of the literature search will be imported into Endnote X9, a literature management software, and after removing duplicate articles, two study members (XTS and XYZ) identified potentially eligible studies by reading the titles and abstracts according to the inclusion–exclusion criteria of the literature, and then two researchers conducted a full-text reading to assess whether the inclusion criteria were met. Any disagreements that arose between reviewers were resolved through discussion or with a third reviewer (HMZ). Assessment of methodological quality Two authors (XTS and KP) independently assessed the quality of the included studies using the 10-item Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) tool [ ], which evaluates the purpose of the study, methodology, recruitment, data collection, researcher reflection, ethical considerations, data analysis, rigor of findings, and appropriateness of the study’s value, ethical considerations, data analysis, rigor of findings, and appropriateness of the study’s value. Any discrepancies in the quality assessment are discussed between the two authors until a consensus is reached. Data extraction Data extraction was carried out using a pre-prepared data extraction form that included: authors, year of publication, country, sample size, phenomenon of interest, study design, methods of data collection and analysis, and main conclusions. Two authors (XTS and XYZ) extracted the data independently, and a third author (HMZ) was responsible for checking the accuracy of the data. The three authors discussed any discrepancies in the extracted data until a consensus was reached. Data synthesis Thematic synthesis was used to generalize and synthesize the qualitative data following the recommendations of the Cochrane Handbook [ ]. Coding and thematic development were carried out in three stages, each of which was independently considered, discussed, and agreed upon by two or more researchers. Data extracted from the results of all included studies were entered verbatim into the NVivo 12 Plus for coding and data management. In the first stage of the analysis, the text of the study was coded. In the second stage, the codes were grouped into logical and meaningful clusters in a hierarchical tree structure to form descriptive themes. Finally, the relationships between the descriptive themes were explained and elaborated, resulting in analytic themes. Thematic integration was done independently by two research team members (XTS and XYZ) who, after discussion, each incorporated their findings into a preliminary thematic framework. This was critically reviewed by a third panelist (HMZ) and revised accordingly by two members. Any disagreement among the three panelists about the final thematic framework was discussed face-to-face until all authors reached a consensus on the thematic framework. A follow-up search of the list of participating literature for the included studies and earlier related reviews identified 2 articles that met the inclusion criteria, and a total of 28 articles were ultimately included in this systematic review. Characteristics of included studies Of the 28 papers included, 6 were in Chinese, and 22 were in English, published between 2005 and 2024, and reporting data from 468 participants from 13 countries (including high- and middle-income countries). The most common were China [ ] and Australia [ ], while other countries included the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Turkey, Canada, Sweden, Norway, Iceland, Switzerland, Denmark, and New Zealand. 2 articles explored patients’ needs during the physical rehabilitation process [ , ], and 12 articles explored patients’ feelings about using an extranet-based rehabilitation platform for physical rehabilitation (5 explored patients’ feelings about utilizing VR for physical rehabilitation [ – ], 2 explored the experience of handheld gaming-based rehabilitation [ , ], and 5 focused on the experience of utilizing a telerehabilitation platform or assistive device for rehabilitation [ – ] 2 studies explored patients’ feelings during intensive upper extremity exercise or high repetition upper extremity exercise [ , ]. The specific characteristics of the included studies are described in Supporting Material 3. Quality of included studies Table (Quality assessment of the included literature) shows the risk of bias ratings of the included studies, with the majority of studies meeting more than 8 of the 10 quality assessment criteria and all of them having some or all of the following values. However, it is worth noting that some of the studies did not describe the methods used for qualitative data analysis, such as thematic or content analysis, or lacked an in-depth description of the analysis process. In addition, few studies considered the relationship between the researcher and the participants, and the researcher did not critically examine his or her role, potential biases, and influences when analyzing and selecting data. These missing details can lead to biased or misleading interpretations of the data, and the lack of relevant details in recruitment strategies in some of the studies further exacerbates the potential for introducing bias. Synthesis results A total of 117 findings were distilled in this study, which were repeatedly read, analyzed, and grouped into 24 new categories, and finally summarized into 4 integrated findings. The relationships between themes and sub-themes are shown in Fig. (The relationships between themes and sub-themes), and a detailed thematic synthesis is shown in Supporting Material 4. Body perception and dynamic adaptation Limb loading During physical rehabilitation, participants often struggle to sustain exercise due to fatigue and pain caused by somatic loading. Six studies have indicated that post-stroke patients frequently experience decreased muscle strength and abnormal muscle tone, along with fatigue and pain during physical rehabilitation [ , , , – ], which can impact the duration and effectiveness of rehabilitation training. Poorly designed rehabilitation equipment Inadequate setup of rehabilitation equipment results in a negative rehabilitation experience for participants. Twelve articles explored physical rehabilitation based on various elements, including Internet technology, and five studies noted that the variety and hierarchical nature of the system often motivated patients. However, technical problems with rehabilitation equipment (e.g., frequent machine malfunctions, poorly configured interfaces resulting in delayed or shifted images) or ergonomic design issues (e.g., overly tight harnesses that cause binding or pain due to friction, bulky sensors, and skin sensitivities) often result in a less than optimal patient experience [ , , , , ], and patients often face various discomforts. Dynamic changes A longitudinal phenomenological study exploring stroke survivors’ perceptions of upper extremity rehabilitation priorities revealed that patients’ rehabilitation priorities shift as rehabilitation progresses [ ]. In the early stages of rehabilitation, patients typically prioritize restoring or improving their ability to walk, focusing on lower extremity function; around six months post-stroke, patients begin to concentrate more on restoring upper extremity function, except for those who cannot walk independently; and by eighteen months post-stroke, all patients aim to restore upper extremity function. Improvement in physical function As the rehabilitation process advances, the limb function of stroke patients improves (e.g., balance function, joint mobility, and gait) with the aid of both spontaneous and specialized rehabilitation [ , , , ]. These improvements enable stroke patients to better integrate into daily life and enhance their self-care and quality of life. Psychological course and emotional experience Negative emotions and social avoidance Due to the sudden onset of the disease, abnormal limb movements, and concerns about the prognosis, patients often experience strong negative psychological effects such as fear and anxiety [ , ]. Before the disease, patients fulfilled various social roles; however, after its onset, their self-care abilities are impaired, leading to a replacement of their original roles and a decrease in family functions. “roles” refer to the positions individuals occupy within social structures (e.g., family, work, community) and the associated behavioral expectations, responsibilities, and obligations (e.g. returning to work or assuming family responsibilities). For stroke patients, the illness often forces significant disruption or transformation of their core social roles. Consequently, patients frequently feel self-blame, resulting in a heavy emotional burden [ , , ]. Additionally, some participants expressed concern about how they were perceived by bystanders. They often felt stigmatized due to physical and speech impairments following a stroke, leading to feelings of low self-esteem and reluctance to engage in daytime outings [ , ]. Desire for restoration of limb function Participants generally conveyed a strong desire for functional recovery, expressing the wish to regain their physical abilities to self-manage and lessen their dependence on others [ , ]. They aspire to return to participation in daily activities, continue their valued hobbies, and resume family and social roles [ , ]. Confusion However, due to a lack of experience in physical rehabilitation and knowledge about the disease, many patients feel confused and helpless during this process. Over time, they may forget the rehabilitation techniques taught by medical staff, causing uncertainty and confusion when they face challenges during rehabilitation exercises [ , , , , , , , ]. This uncertainty not only amplifies the patients’ psychological burden but also impacts their rehabilitation outcomes and adherence. Furthermore, three studies indicate that patients often exhibit psychological dependence when confronted with multiple rehabilitation options, with some typically following the decisions of family heads, elderly parents adhering to their children’s advice, and others delegating decision-making to therapists [ , , ]. Fear and self-doubt Stroke patients frequently endure a psychological state of fear intertwined with self-doubt during rehabilitation. This state is marked by significant uncertainty regarding falls and other adverse events, low self-efficacy caused by post-stroke limb dysfunction [ , , ], fear of causing injury or inconvenience to others [ ], and apprehension towards new rehabilitation methods [ , , ]. Lack of therapeutic care Three studies noted that the transition from therapist-led to patient-directed rehabilitation occurred prematurely after discharge [ , , ]. As treatment frequency diminishes, patients often feel unsupported, neglected, and abandoned by healthcare services. Loss of patience Gait rehabilitation for stroke is lengthy and varies by individual, and during this period, patients may have insufficient understanding of their condition or overly high expectations for their rehabilitation progress. Therefore, when actual outcomes fall short of their expectations, it frequently leads to frustration [ , , , ]. Some participants expressed resistance to rehabilitation as they observed no immediate improvement in their limb functionality and considered rehabilitation futile or unattainable [ , , ]. Additionally, a singular rehabilitation strategy often leads to boredom and frustration, causing patients to lose patience during the prolonged rehabilitation process [ , , ]. However, with the assisted rehabilitation by healthcare professionals, the patients’ limb functions gradually improved, which enhanced their self-confidence in the rehabilitation process and made them participate more actively in rehabilitation exercises. Additionally, some participants recognized the beneficial role of religious beliefs throughout their recovery journey [ ], viewing them as a source of liberation and hope and offering spiritual support to patients. Multidimensional motivations and facilitators Positive feedback Positive feedback, whether it is verbal encouragement from the therapist, visual indicators of progress (e.g., walking speed/distance), or automatic rewards in rehabilitation techniques (e.g., ‘good job’ messages, points), is a powerful facilitator that helps to enhance self-efficacy promoting a sense of accomplishment related to achieving goals. “Self-efficacy” refers to an individual’s confidence and belief in their capability to successfully execute specific behaviors and achieve desired outcomes. In the rehabilitation context, it specifically denotes the patient’s confidence in their ability to effectively engage in and adhere to rehabilitation exercises, overcome challenges, and ultimately achieve functional recovery. This information provides them with a clearer understanding and higher expectations of their rehabilitation progress [ , , , ]. Integrated incentives and feedback mechanisms within rehabilitation platforms further reinforce this confidence, preventing discouragement during the recovery process [ , ]. Diverse external support Physical, emotional, and social support from medical staff, peers, family, and the community motivates persistence [ , , ]. They not only offer essential physical assistance but also foster a sense of care and understanding through encouragement and support, thereby enhancing patients’ motivation to face recovery challenges positively. Group-based activities further cultivate a sense of belonging, transforming rehabilitation into a collectively meaningful endeavor [ , , , , , , , ]. Participants found communication with others facing similar illnesses to be beneficial, as they exchanged firsthand knowledge of stroke and rehabilitation and sought mutual motivation and psychological support. Participants frequently felt more secure and confident exercising with a peer group and being part of a team, which not only fostered a positive sense of connection but also encouraged a positive outlook on life. Challenging design Hierarchical and competitive designs (e.g., leaderboards, increasing difficulty) tap into patients’ intrinsic motivation by designing rehabilitation as an engaging pursuit of achievement [ – , ]. Task designs (e.g., virtual flight simulations) are often more engaging through real-time reward cycles (e.g., points, visual feedback) and immersive tasks (e.g., virtual flight simulations) [ , , , ]. Internet-based rehabilitation platforms (e.g., virtual reality, tablet-based games) are often considered more innovative and interesting than traditional approaches. Goal setting and sense of achievement Setting clear goals and gaining a sense of accomplishment positively affect a patient’s recovery. Goals based on the patient’s identity (e.g., beliefs, values, or culture) and meaningful aspects of life (e.g., relationships, hobbies, and occupations) transform abstract recovery into value-driven action [ , ]. Patients gain motivation from self-observed improvements in functioning (e.g., improved performance at daily tasks), which validates the achievability of goals [ , , , ], in contrast to unmonitored progress, which leads to frustration and weakens the nature of adherence [ ]. Positive emotional attitudes and personality traits Positive emotional attitudes and personality traits enhance patients’ motivation to recover, influencing recovery outcomes. Inherent traits like humor and perseverance function as psychological buffers, enabling patients to reframe setbacks. These traits also drive rehabilitation integration, embedding exercises into daily routines (e.g., using stairs as therapy) to reduce willpower dependency [ , , ]. Avoiding disability labeling and functional degradation Avoiding disability labeling and functional decline emerged as crucial motivations for participants to continue their rehabilitation. They strongly rejected the stigma and pity associated with disability, wanting to be recognized as capable individuals rather than disabled. This mindset motivates them to challenge themselves continually and strive to regain function, preserving their dignity and independence. Additionally, concerns about functional decline further motivate adherence in stroke patients, who hope to maintain their current functioning and independence through ongoing rehabilitation and thus avoid falling into a detrimental cycle of functional loss [ , ]. Unmet needs and directions for optimizing intervention strategies Convenient and continuous demand for rehabilitation services Nine studies point to patients’ desire for convenient and consistent rehabilitation services that provide flexibility to practice according to their daily living plans [ , , , , , , , , ]. Although municipalities offer a variety of services, access to them is often complicated by time or frequency constraints [ ], particularly for patients in rural and remote areas, where distance, travel time, therapist turnover rates, and other limitations render participation in rehabilitation training very challenging or impossible [ , , ]. They expressed frustration with the commuting time involved, and stroke survivors showed a strong desire for rehabilitation services closer to home or available within their communities. Simultaneously, patients are eager for post-discharge follow-up, professional guidance, and to maintain close contact with healthcare professionals for improved rehabilitation outcomes [ , , ]. Additionally, varying literacy and skill levels among patients led some participants to express concerns about difficulties with technology due to hardware limitations or personal conditions. Some elderly stroke patients found operating tablets and other devices too complicated and indicated a need for training support or technical guidance from medical staff [ , ]. Access to rehabilitation information and resources Low accessibility of rehabilitation-related information, a lack of supporting rehabilitation facilities, irrational design of rehabilitation assistance appliances, and a shortage of community workers hinder patients from undergoing limb function rehabilitation. Stroke patients and their families often remain unaware of the correct methods for functional exercise after leaving medical or rehabilitation institutions, and the out-of-hospital exercise routines lack professional guidance and team support from medical staff. In contrast, information regarding stroke physical rehabilitation in daily life and on the internet is limited, generalized, and hardly accessible [ , ]. With an extended discharge time, patients often feel uncertain about their rehabilitation and struggle to effectively resolve challenges encountered during rehabilitation exercises, which negatively impacts their adherence to rehabilitation and its effectiveness. Patients hope that hospitals or rehabilitation institutions can provide professional and personalized rehabilitation guidance and offer more specific information about the pros and cons of rehabilitation programs so they can choose a suitable rehabilitation method for themselves [ , , ]. Furthermore, the lack of rehabilitation opportunities and the inadequate facilities or assistive devices have created a scarcity of opportunities for patients, and stroke patients are eager for more exercise instruments, devices, and venues that cater to their needs to aid them in performing rehabilitation exercises [ , , , , , ]. Individualized rehabilitation guidance Five studies reported participants’ desire for personalized guidance from healthcare professionals during recovery [ , , , , ]. Participants reported a lack of targeted guidance on how to perform the exercises or how long to continue them. During rehabilitation, patients sometimes experience fatigue and even severe pain, yet they often choose to tolerate this discomfort, seeking help from healthcare professionals only when it becomes unbearable. This endurance stems not only from the pain but also partly from the fear of being perceived as “weak” or “uncooperative” by others [ ]. There is a strong desire among patients for healthcare professionals to pay more attention to their individual needs and to develop and adapt rehabilitation treatments to each patient’s specific situation. Socialization and group interaction between patients with similar experiences Four studies emphasized the participants’ need for social and group interactions with others who have similar experiences [ , , , ]. Group therapy is recognized as a more cost-effective form of long-term support and treatment, where stroke survivors can mutually encourage and resource each other. Survivors expressed enthusiasm for the prospect of socializing and exercising together, stating they hoped dedicated spaces, such as activity rooms or public fitness centers, could be arranged for socializing and learning from one another and fellow survivors, which could aid in recovery [ , ]. Economic support and policy guarantees Patients often experience varying degrees of limb dysfunction post-stroke, which may lead to loss of financial income as they can no longer engage in their former occupations. Additionally, post-stroke treatment, medication, and rehabilitation represent a chronic process that demands long-term adherence and incurs high costs, ultimately deterring most patients. Many have expressed feelings of helplessness and distress regarding having to abandon treatment due to financial pressure [ , , , , ]. Patients generally hope that the government can offer more subsidies to reduce treatment and rehabilitation costs, particularly advocating for the inclusion of rehabilitation-related expenses within the scope of health insurance reimbursement to alleviate the financial burden on individuals and their families [ , ]. Real-time feedback and intelligent adjustments Eight studies noted participants’ desire to monitor their progress and receive timely feedback throughout the recovery process [ , , , , , , , ]. Whether through online telerehabilitation using an extranet platform or offline, face-to-face rehabilitation with a therapist, participants expressed a desire to visualize their exercises and utilize visual and auditory feedback to gauge whether they need to intensify their efforts or adjust their approach. As progress in rehabilitation is often gradual, effective monitoring and feedback help them recognize if they are proceeding correctly and track their improvements, which can enhance their confidence and motivate them further. Discussion Patients’ self-efficacy in rehabilitation increases as they perceive improvements in their physical abilities during the recovery process. Physical rehabilitation that utilizes Internet technology, such as handheld games or virtual reality, is more engaging and convenient than traditional face-to-face rehabilitation sessions with a therapist [ ]. However, patients’ attitudes towards and acceptance of digital technology often vary widely, likely due to factors like varying levels of education and age differences [ ]. Elderly stroke patients with lower literacy frequently feel confused, especially during the initial phase of using these technologies [ ]. Therefore, when implementing Internet-based interventions, healthcare professionals should take into account the diversity among patients from different cultural backgrounds and age groups, focusing specifically on the acceptance of older stroke patients with lower literacy levels. Additionally, poorly designed rehabilitation equipment can lead to unpleasant experiences for patients [ , , ]. In the future, when designing limb rehabilitation aids for stroke patients, it is essential to prioritize creating aids that are compact and user-friendly, with appropriate ergonomics and a clear, simple interface. It is important to recognize that there are variations in the focus on upper and lower limb function among stroke patients at different rehabilitation stages. It has been suggested that in the early stages of rehabilitation, patients often prioritize lower limb function to restore or improve their walking ability; around six months post-stroke, patients begin to shift their focus toward recovering upper limb function, except for those unable to walk independently; and by eighteen months post-stroke, all patients concentrate on regaining upper limb function [ ]. This pattern may relate to the evolution of an individual’s core needs as described in Maslow’s hierarchy of needs theory. In the early rehabilitation stage, patients’ core needs focus on physiological safety, which is evident in their fixation on gait recovery, motivated by fear of falling and embarrassment of over-relying on others for toileting. In the middle stage, patients’ core needs shift towards belongingness and respect, reflected in their desire for independence in managing daily personal tasks (e.g., shaving, cooking) to avoid appearing entirely dependent. In the late stage of rehabilitation, the core need becomes self-actualization, expressed through the pursuit of occupational rehabilitation or the return to hobbies. This indicates that healthcare professionals should not only recognize the visible dysfunctions of patients but also understand the dynamically shifting core needs underlying them. Stroke patients face complex and diverse psychological and social challenges during the rehabilitation process. Studies have shown that disease onset, abnormal limb function, and prognostic concerns together induce strong negative psychological experiences in patients [ , ]. These psychological reactions not only stem from the disease itself but are also closely related to the social environment. The disruption of patients’ social roles has led to a dual psychological impact: on the one hand, the loss of self-worth resulting from the weakening of family functions; on the other hand, the stigma attached to post-stroke dysfunction has created a vicious cycle of “self-stigma-social withdrawal”, whereby patients’ social participation is limited. Medical professionals need to help patients rebuild their sense of self-worth and improve their psychological status through early screening and timely intervention from a biopsychosocial perspective. In addition, patients’ lack of knowledge about rehabilitation and the uncertainty created by forgetting methods often place them in a passive role in the decision-making process. Especially in the family decision-making model, elderly patients tend to follow the advice of their children or therapists [ , ]. This phenomenon of psychological dependence also reveals the inadequacy of the stroke rehabilitation education system. Medical personnel can adopt a phased approach to education, focusing on disease mechanisms and prognosis in the acute phase, and rehabilitation skills (e.g., mobility skills) in the recovery phase, as well as using tools such as videos and graphic manuals to reduce forgetfulness. To address the passive decision-making tendency of elderly patients, medical staff can use ‘decision-making aids’ (e.g., option lists, risk comparison charts, and pros and cons analysis tables) to help patients understand the advantages and disadvantages of different rehabilitation options, encouraging them to participate in developing personalized training plans to enhance their autonomy [ ]. Seeing progress and receiving positive feedback are factors that promote recovery, and ongoing monitoring and evaluation are key to long-term adherence. Many studies indicate that patients feel “marginalized” and “abandoned” after being discharged from hospitals, often facing challenges such as unclear channels of help, lack of professional support, uncertain progress, and difficulty confirming whether they are following the right pathway. This can lead to a loss of patience and a tendency to give up during the long-term recovery process [ , , ]. Consequently, they lose patience and opt to abandon long-term rehabilitation efforts. In the future, we should enhance the “hospital-community-family” three-way linkage extended care model, improve the social support system for full-cycle rehabilitation of stroke, and provide multi-channel, easily accessible professional support resources [ , ]. Implementing a regular monitoring and evaluation mechanism can provide patients with timely positive and clear feedback, allowing them to see the progress of their rehabilitation. At the same time, extranet-based rehabilitation platforms or assistive devices should improve their monitoring and feedback mechanisms so that patients can feel in real time whether their rehabilitation actions are correct and make timely adjustments based on the feedback content. Additionally, presenting patients with stage-by-stage assessment reports can help them visualize the extent of improvement in their physical function and the progress made, thereby enhancing their confidence in adhering to long-term rehabilitation [ ]. Interaction and social support among peers with similar experiences can positively impact a patient’s recovery process [ ]. Peer socialization promotes learning and communication among patients, and in group therapy, they can observe each other’s recovery progress, which motivates them to work harder. They can also share their experiences and insights to learn from each other, fostering positive interactions. This aligns with several studies [ – ]. In the future, it is essential to provide dedicated rehabilitation exercise spaces, organize diverse group activities, strengthen rehabilitation education and publicity, and establish peer support networks among stroke patients, utilizing both online and offline methods. For instance, organizing rehabilitation lectures and experience-sharing sessions can promote communication and interaction among patients, enrich their rehabilitation experience, and enhance their sense of social belonging [ ]. A systematic review of older adults’ participation in dance fitness games showed that those who participated as a group reported higher adherence and a stronger sense of belonging compared to individuals who participated alone [ ]. Therefore, designing future extranet-based rehabilitation platforms or assistive devices should include social elements and create rehabilitation devices or games that allow multiple participants to enhance patient compliance. Introduction Migraine is the second most disabling disorder worldwide and incurs enormous societal costs, estimated to exceed €50 billion per year in the EU alone. , Frequent migraine attacks warrant preventive treatment. A multitude of preventive pharmacological options are available; however, there are several barriers to effective treatment. For instance, one study reported that over two-thirds of patients discontinued their prophylactic migraine medication after six months, and more than 80% after a year, due to either a lack of efficacy or adverse reactions. Several non-pharmacological behavioral interventions for migraine, such as biofeedback, have been highlighted as non-invasive prophylactic treatment regimens with a low risk of negative side effects, which can be an alternative or adjunct to pharmacological therapies. Biofeedback combined with relaxation training is listed with Grade A level evidence for migraine prevention in the 2000 guidelines from the American Academy of Neurology. This has been continued in the updated 2021 American Headache Society consensus statement, which also suggests mobile health (mHealth) application-based approaches for delivering biobehavioural treatments to increase patient access and participation. Biofeedback utilizes technologies and equipment to monitor physiological processes that are usually considered involuntary and modulated without conscious awareness. Presented with real-time feedback on these processes, users can learn to exercise control over them, which in turn has a beneficial effect on the migraine symptom burden. Despite its effectiveness, biofeedback has limited accessibility. The high financial costs of having a therapist instructing the procedure, necessary equipment, and patient travelling costs are likely to contribute to this. To our knowledge, no therapist-independent migraine biofeedback treatment with proven efficacy is currently available. To address this gap, a multimodal biofeedback system, the Cerebri system, has been developed for therapist-independent home-based use. Unique to this product, the Cerebri application (app) seamlessly integrates three biofeedback modalities: heart rate variability (HRV), temperature, and electromyography (EMG), making it a comprehensive, home-based solution for non-pharmacological migraine management. The device is a product of a thorough development process, including a hardware feasibility study and three development studies on progenitor versions of the system with short test periods. – In addition, prior to the initiation of this trial, a feasibility study with 3-month follow-up was performed. Primary efficacy endpoint The primary endpoint is the change in the mean number of migraine days from baseline to the last 28-day period (week 9–12) during the treatment phase in the treatment group compared to the wait-list control group. Secondary efficacy endpoints The key secondary endpoint analyses are changes in mean number of migraine days in week 1–4 and week 5–8, change in mean migraine intensity, proportion of 30% responders, change in acute migraine drug treatment use, and change in subject-reported headache-related disability. Exploratory and descriptive endpoints include changes in weekly migraine days, mean headache days per 28-day period, eDiary and biofeedback session adherence, and mean Patient Global Impression of Change (PGI-C) scores. Additionally, changes in the mean number of migraine days during the extended biofeedback period will be assessed. Safety endpoints Description of the frequency and severity of treatment-emergent adverse events (AEs), adverse device effects (ADEs), serious adverse device effects (SADEs), and unexpected serious adverse side effects (USADEs) is included. In the case of pregnant participants, at inclusion or acknowledged during participation, no additional monitoring of maternal or fetal health is instituted. One sensor is attached to the index finger and measures HRV and peripheral skin temperature. All training is delivered in a standardised, app-based format without individualised or therapist-led instruction. Discussion To the best of our knowledge, this is the first pivotal randomized controlled trial (RCT) with an adequate sample size to properly evaluate the efficacy of home-based biofeedback treatment in patients with episodic migraine. A 2022 systematic review of digital headache interventions identified only two RCTs evaluating biofeedback apps for migraine. Both were pilot studies with small sample sizes and did not show statistically significant between-group differences in important headache related outcomes. , The uniqueness of Cerebri is that it combines three different biofeedback modalities, whereas traditional treatments typically use one parameter. , In addition, recent app-based solutions have applied one modality. , , Different modalities may benefit different users; for example, some users might find it easier to influence their finger temperature, whereas others might prefer muscle tension as their main source of biofeedback. Different modalities also display different responses over time. The non-invasiveness of the Cerebri-system is advantageous in several ways. First, it enables the patients to safely perform the procedure themselves. Second, it means the risk profile is relatively low, with the most severe identified risks being electrical failure in the sensors or charger, skin contact-dependent allergic reactions from the sensor material, and risks related to information security and privacy. All the identified risks were met using an appropriate mitigation strategy. Third, a wider spectrum of patients qualifies for study inclusion; notably, women of childbearing potential who do not use highly effective contraceptives, as well as those who are pregnant or breastfeeding. The BioCer trial is not blinded and employs a waitlist control. In a previous sham-controlled trial involving adolescents that tested an earlier version of the Cerebri system, the investigators encountered difficulties in developing a biofeedback sham that effectively imitated authentic biofeedback. False feedback was easily detected by the user, compromising the integrity of the blinding protocol. Conversely, attempts to distort the biofeedback signal by introducing minor “errors” resulted in a sham signal that was “too similar” to true biofeedback, potentially inducing a treatment effect. In addition to the practical challenge of developing an appropriate sham signal, there are significant ethical concerns associated with providing false biofeedback to participants. These concerns include the potential exacerbation of migraines. Indeed, in theory, introducing a false biofeedback signal could lead to mislearning, in which subjects inadvertently adapt incorrect or maladaptive responses based on what they believe to be true biofeedback. Nevertheless, the absence of blinding is a limitation, as it prevents assessment of the placebo effect. We believe that the effectiveness of Cerebri depends on achieving adequate user satisfaction and adherence to ensure optimal results. However, a recurrent challenge for smartphone-based biofeedback is its low adherence. A pilot study in adolescents of a progenitor version of Cerebri reported poor adherence, with a mere 40% of planned biofeedback sessions completed during weeks 5-8 of the study. Similar adherence challenges have been reported for smartphone-based systems. In the feasibility study of the current Cerebri system proceeding this trial, biofeedback adherence was also low, declining from 80% in week 1-4 to 20% in week 9-12. Several usability and software issues were identified and addressed before trial initiation. To improve the usability of the Cerebri mobile app, additional data were added to the diary and visualized in graphs to provide users with better tools to keep track of their headaches and to compare headache data with biofeedback data directly. In addition, the app content was revised and instructions were improved based on reported use errors or misinterpretations. Based on user insights, the app interface during the biofeedback sessions was tailored to ensure that the biofeedback was performed correctly. Furthermore, the algorithm for calculating the HRV score was modified to compensate for drifting biofeedback scores resulting from frequency leakage from the low-to high-frequency domains of the HR wave. Some drifting still occurs, but it is deemed acceptable as the users are considered unable to observe this. The project utilized existing technology in the market, and as the concept developed, custom-made sensors and a more advanced biofeedback app interface were developed over the course of several years. Clinical testing of feasibility and usability continued to show positive feedback from the patients , ; hence, the project continued to validate the clinical effect of Cerebri. Introduction Epilepsy is one of the most common neurological disorders, characterized by recurrent seizures that significantly impact patients’ quality of life. Despite advances in antiseizure medications, achieving optimal seizure control remains challenging for many patients. Brivaracetam (BRV), a propyl analog of levetiracetam, functions as an antiseizure medication through its high-affinity binding to synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A). The U.S. Food and Drug Administration first approved BRV in 2016 as an adjunctive treatment for focal onset seizures in patients aged 16 years and older. Subsequently, in 2017, its approval was extended to include monotherapy for focal onset seizures in the same age group. Further expansion of its indications occurred in 2018, allowing its use in patients aged 4 years and older, and in 2021, it was approved for patients aged 1 month and older. In Europe, BRV is currently approved as an adjunctive therapy for focal onset seizures, with or without secondary generalization, in patients aged 2 years and older. In South Korea, the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety approved BRV in 2019 in the form of oral solution and film-coated tablets as adjunctive therapy for focal onset seizures, with or without secondary generalization, in adult and adolescent patients aged 16 years and older with epilepsy. However, despite regulatory approval, BRV has yet to be introduced to the South Korean market. This review aimed to provide a comprehensive analysis of BRV’s pharmacological properties, efficacy, tolerability, and safety profile, synthesizing data from clinical trials and real-world evidence. Pharmacodynamic properties BRV belongs to the racetam family and, like levetiracetam (LEV), binds to the SV2A ligand. However, it interacts with a different binding site or conformational state of SV2A. Additionally, BRV exhibits a more selective binding affinity for the SV2A protein, with an affinity 15–30 times higher than that of LEV. SV2A is a transmembrane glycoprotein present in synaptic vesicles in the central nervous system, playing a crucial role in the exocytosis of neurotransmitters from vesicles. BRV inhibits this exocytosis, leading to a reduction in the release of excitatory neurotransmitters. It enters recycling synaptic vesicles, causing a frequency-dependent decrease in synaptic transmission at concentrations 100 times lower than those required for LEV and more effectively slows synaptic vesicle mobilization. Initial animal studies suggested that BRV might inhibit voltage-gated sodium channels; however, subsequent studies revealed that BRV does not affect voltage-gated sodium currents in cornu ammonis 1 (CA1) neurons or sustained repetitive firing in cortical and CA1 neurons. , At therapeutic brain concentrations, BRV did not modulate inhibitory or excitatory postsynaptic ligand-gated ion channels in mouse hippocampal neurons, supporting evidence that its antiepileptic effects stem from its selective action on the presynaptic SV2A protein. Pharmacokinetic properties Absorption and distribution BRV is rapidly absorbed in the intestines following oral administration, exhibiting nearly 100% bioavailability. It demonstrates linear kinetics, with plasma concentrations increasing proportionally to the dose administered. When delivered intravenously, a 100 mg dose of BRV exhibited similar bioavailability to 50 and 100 mg oral tablets. Although the 100 mg intravenous formulation showed a faster rise in plasma levels and a dose-normalized Cmax that was 28% and 21% higher than the 50 and 100 mg oral tablets, respectively, the plasma concentration profiles became similar after the first hour. As a result, the intravenous dose achieved bioequivalence with the oral formulations in terms of overall exposure, as measured by the area under the plasma concentration-time curve from time zero to the last measurable concentration and extrapolated to infinity. These findings suggest that no dose adjustment is necessary when switching between oral and intravenous administration. Intravenous BRV was well tolerated in a phase III randomized, placebo-controlled trial ( NCT01405508 ) involving 105 epilepsy patients aged 16–70 years with focal or generalized epilepsy uncontrolled by one or two antiseizure medications, with treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) reported in 70.6% of patients initiating intravenous treatment and 66.0% of those transitioning from oral BRV. The incidence of TEAEs was comparable between 2-minute bolus (71.2%) and 15-minute infusion (65.4%) administration methods. Injection-related TEAEs were observed in 9.6% of patients receiving bolus and 11.5% of those receiving infusion. Plasma concentrations were marginally higher in the bolus group following the first dose but became comparable across all groups after the final dose. These findings indicate that intravenous BRV is a viable alternative for patients unable to take oral formulations. BRV is lipophilic and rapidly crosses the blood-brain barrier through passive diffusion, binding to its target site, SV2A. Preclinical studies demonstrated that BRV enters the brain faster than LEV, resulting in a quicker onset of seizure control. This was evidenced by rodent models and supported by positron emission tomography (PET) studies in nonhuman primates. Using the SV2A PET tracer 11 C-UCB-J, previous research evaluated brain penetration and occupancy time courses for BRV and LEV at therapeutic doses. In a previous study involving 13 healthy volunteers, BRV demonstrated faster tracer displacement half-time (18 minutes for 100 mg) than LEV (28 minutes for 1,500 mg). It also displayed higher receptor occupancy and a significantly lower half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ), suggesting greater potency. IC 50 reflects the concentration required to inhibit 50% of target activity. BRV has a half-life of approximately 8–9 hours, a plasma protein binding rate of less than 20%, and a volume of distribution of 0.5–0.6 L/kg. Steady-state concentrations are achieved within 2 days of repeated dosing. While high-fat meals can delay the time to peak plasma concentration (0.5–3.5 hours) and reduce maximum plasma concentration, they do not affect the AUC, ensuring that overall absorption remains consistent. Metabolism BRV undergoes extensive metabolism in the liver, primarily via hydrolysis of its acetamide group, producing a carboxylic acid metabolite. This is followed by hydroxylation mediated by cytochrome P450 (CYP) 2C9. A secondary metabolic pathway involves beta-oxidation of the propyl side chain via CYP2C19, resulting in a hydroxy metabolite. A combination of these pathways leads to the formation of a hydroxy-acid metabolite. The three primary metabolites (acid, hydroxy, and hydroxy-acid) are pharmacologically inactive. Although the levels of these metabolites increase in patients with reduced renal clearance, this does not result in significant adverse effects, and dose adjustment is typically not required. However, this conclusion is based on studies that excluded patients undergoing dialysis; therefore, caution is advised in this population. Conversely, BRV exposure increases by 50–60% in patients with hepatic impairment due to altered biotransformation, including reduced CYP-dependent hydroxylation and increased CYP-independent acid metabolite formation. Consequently, a dose reduction is recommended in patients with hepatic impairment. Elimination BRV is primarily excreted through the kidneys, with over 90% of the administered dose eliminated within 2 days. Of this, 8.6% is excreted in the urine as unmetabolized BRV. Pharmacokinetic drug interactions BRV has a low potential to affect the activity of cytochrome P450 enzymes. A study analyzing five randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled efficacy trials reported that BRV does not influence the steady-state plasma concentrations of commonly prescribed antiseizure medications, including levetiracetam, lacosamide, lamotrigine, phenobarbital, pregabalin, phenytoin, topiramate, valproate, and zonisamide. In a phase I open-label study, BRV co-administration with carbamazepine did not significantly alter carbamazepine AUC over a dosing interval but increased levels of carbamazepine-epoxide, an active metabolite. BRV inhibited the in vitro hydrolysis of carbamazepine-epoxide in human hepatocytes, demonstrating an IC 50 value of 8.2 μM. Carbamazepine modestly decreased BRV AUC while increasing its oxidative metabolism. A post-hoc analysis of pooled data from phase III studies indicated that the increase in carbamazepine-epoxide levels did not lead to clinically significant adverse events, suggesting that dose adjustments are not necessary when BRV and carbamazepine are co-administered. In addition to interactions mediated by metabolic enzymes, the potential influence of BRV on drug transporters has also been investigated. In vitro studies suggest that BRV does not meaningfully inhibit or induce key transporters, including P-glycoprotein (P-gp). As a result, it is unlikely that BRV would alter the P-gp-mediated efflux of common substrates such as digoxin or newer oral anticoagulants, including apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, and rivaroxaban. Collectively, these findings support the notion that BRV carries a low risk of clinically relevant drug transporter-mediated drug interactions. Doses of BRV at 400 mg/day, when taken with oral contraceptives (OCs) in healthy women (n=24), led to a 27% reduction in plasma levels of ethinyl estradiol and a 23% reduction in levonorgestrel levels. 1. Introduction In repeated measures studies, researchers observe multiple responses on a set of independent sampling units. The repeated measurements may be longitudinal (across time), spatial (across location), or multivariate (on different scales). Outcome data are missing when a measurement is not observed at a particular planned occasion. The chance that an observation is missing may vary across measurements, and missingness may be correlated across measurements. Both the amount and the pattern of missing outcome data can affect power in repeated measures studies. Such complex missing data patterns occur frequently in biomedical studies. For example, in a randomized controlled clinical trial of physiotherapy in patients with Parkinson’s disease ( ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01257945 ) ( ), increasing dropout over a 16 month follow-up period produced missing measurements of physical function. In this study, the chance that a data point was missing appeared to be unrelated to either outcomes or covariates. Published power approximations use assumptions that do not match the complex missing data patterns like the one in the Parkinson’s disease study. , ) assumed no missing data. use local alternative distributions which rely on asymptotic assumptions for accuracy. Further compounding the issues with local alternatives, the use of GEE estimates has been shown to suffer from inflated Type I error rates in small samples, weakening its otherwise general appeal ( ). accounts for missing data in their power approximation, but they too assume local alternative distributions. accounts for missing data and uses a noncentral F -distribution proposed by , ), but they assume that every response was independently and equally likely to be missing. To counteract these challenges, we provide power approximations that accommodate complex missing data processes characterized by a conditional linear model ( ). We modify a noncentral F power approximation for a class of mixed models with no missing data described by , ) and . The modifications incorporate the expected value of one of several missing data summary statistics ( ; ; ). The choice of which missing data summary statistic to use depends on whether scientists plan complete - or observed -case data analytic approaches. The complete-case approach uses only independent sampling units with all measurements present. The observed-case approach uses any independent sampling unit with at least one measurement. There are two missing data summary statistics in particular that we favor for these objective analyses. The work applies to a broad and useful subset of missing processes, models and hypothesis tests. The data are assumed to be missing completely at random (MCAR) ( ). Under the MCAR assumption, the distribution of the missing responses does not depend on any of the observed outcomes, unobserved outcomes or explanatory variables. The models are assumed to be a class of general linear mixed models ( ) referred to as balanced linear mixed models ( ; ). A general linear mixed model is a balanced linear mixed model if it can be expressed as an equivalent general linear multivariate model when there is no missing data. We restrict attention to the Wald test and the Kenward-Roger reference distribution due to its equivalence with a Hotelling-Lawley trace test ( ). We use a covariance estimator that assumes an unstructured correlation pattern between responses which has been shown to be quite favorable in clinical trial settings with random dropout ( ). Balanced linear mixed models fulfill the following criteria. For a particular independent sampling unit, the predictors have the same value for all outcomes. In addition, each independent sampling unit has the same number of planned predictors and the same error covariance matrix. In balanced linear mixed models with no missing data, each independent sampling unit has the same number and type of planned outcome measurements. In this manuscript, we relax the last assumption, and allow for missing data. Discussion Missing data occurs everywhere in biomedical research, from longitudinal epidemiologic observational studies to randomized controlled clinical trials. Missing data can strongly affect the power of biomedical research studies and thus the choice of sample size. If the sample size is larger than needed, too many participants are exposed to the potential risk of research. If the sample size is smaller than needed, resources, investigator and participant time are wasted on a study that has insufficient statistical power to answer the question of interest. Accurate power and sample size calculations must take into account the chance of missing data. The methods proposed in the current work allow power calculations for some important classes of models and missing data processes. We consider balanced linear mixed models and the Wald test with Kenward-Rogers degrees of freedom. We also used a flexible model of the missing data process to allow us to examine how different missing data patterns affect the results of the power analysis. We consider balanced linear mixed models and the Wald test with Kenward-Rogers degrees of freedom. We also used a flexible model of the missing data process to allow us to examine how different missing data patterns affect the results of the power analysis. The work extends previous power approximations for data without missing values ( ; ) and for data with values missing completely at random with equal probability ( ). The new methods accommodate complex missing data processes ( ) to better mirror processes likely to occur in real repeated measures studies. The missing data processes we consider allow a different chance of missingness for each measurement in a repeated measures study. In addition, the missing data processes allow for the chance of missingness for one measurement to be correlated with the chance of missingness of another measurement. We provide different power approximations for the complete- and observed-case data analytic approaches, both of which are commonly used in biomedical research. The approximation has adequate accuracy for the scenarios scientists care about the most, with true power between 0.8 and 0.95. The error in the power approximation is in the second decimal place. A version of the approximations described here will be included in Version 3 of GLIMMPSE ( ), available at SampleSizeShop.org . The GLIMMPSE power and sample size software for multilevel and longitudinal studies is user-friendly, point-and-click and available to run without cost from a web browser. Users who prefer R code to implement the methods may request a copy from the authors. To approximate power for a study with no missing data, a scientist needs to specify the Type I error rate, predictor matrix, error variance, between- and within-independent sampling unit contrasts and sample size. To conduct an accurate power calculation with outcome data missing completely at random, a scientist must, in addition, choose an appropriate missing data process. The choice should depend on the scientist’s assumptions about the missing data process. The conditional linear missing data process can accommodate several assumptions, including autoregressive and unstructured correlation structures. Estimates for the chance that the response is missing at each measurement, and the correlation between missingness at each measurement can be obtained from literature reports, from previous unpublished data, or from an understanding of the rationale for missing data in a certain study design, disease state, or treatment regimen. While the power approximations cover a useful set of models and missing data processes, there are limitations to the work. First, the assumption that the data are missing completely at random (MCAR) may not hold. The MCAR assumption means that the chance that a response is missing does not depend on observed data, including covariates. Secondly, the manuscript only proposes power analyses for balanced linear mixed models with Gaussian outcomes. This means that the results may not hold for studies with mistimed data, time-dependent covariates or non-Gaussian outcomes. In future work, we hope to develop a maximum likelihood approach to estimate marginal missingness, and correlation between missingness from completed studies. It would be useful to develop a corresponding likelihood ratio test to aid scientists in characterizing a missing data process. We also plan to relax the assumption that the outcome data are missing completely at random. We hope to consider a larger class of models and outcomes, including non-linear mixed models, and binary and Poisson distributed outcomes. It is important to consider how power calculations are affected by the use of observed (and hence random) percentages of missingness at each measurement drawn from previous experiments. An additional open question is how to compute confidence intervals for power for studies with missing data. For ethical reasons, some investigators may prefer to consider quantiles of power, rather than power calculated for an expected amount of missingness. Introduction Seizures affect approximately 7 in 10 000 children before the age of 2 years and 1 in 500 before 5 years and are often associated with developmental delay. An increasing number of causative genes are recognised in what is emerging as an overlapping group of disorders with varying prevalence and severity of seizures, developmental delay and, in some cases, dysmorphic features or congenital malformations. Standard diagnostic approaches include biochemical and enzyme analysis for neurometabolic disorders, MRI brain imaging and genome-wide microarray analysis. Where these investigations do not identify a structural brain anomaly, biomarkers for a neurometabolic disorder, or chromosomal CNV, diagnosis is often challenging and has traditionally been dependent on the recognition of a characteristic phenotype followed by targeted single-gene testing. Examples include SCN1A -related seizure disorders and classical Rett syndrome ( MECP2 ). With increasing published literature on the wide spectrum of molecular aetiologies in these patients, targeted gene testing has allowed diagnosis in an increasing number of patients. Children with early-onset seizures and severe developmental delay (early infantile epileptic encephalopathy (EIEE)) can often be classified according to their electroclinical phenotype, for example, Ohtahara syndrome, West syndrome and epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (EIMFS). For some cases, accurate EIEE syndrome classification can assist in the identification of causative genes. Similarly, the recognition of a number of neurobehavioural and dysmorphic syndromes also helps identify disease-causing genes in some individuals. However, for many cases, clinical prediction of causative genes is challenging due to genetic heterogeneity, phenotypic pleiotropy, and for some patients, the phenotype is not sufficiently distinctive to accurately predict the causative gene. In such cases, sequential single-gene testing is time-consuming, costly and often unsuccessful. With the increasing availability of next-generation sequencing technologies, it is becoming possible to rely less on targeted single-gene analysis. This has the potential to improve diagnostic rates. It can also clarify and broaden the phenotypic spectrum of genes by reducing ascertainment bias. We, therefore, chose to explore the diagnostic utility and genotype–phenotype insights provided by analysis of a panel of 46 genes in 400 patients with early-onset seizures and/or severe developmental delay. Methods Patients and samples Four hundred patients with early-onset seizure disorders and/or severe developmental delay were referred and consented for gene panel testing by a paediatric neurologist or clinical geneticist, from a number of tertiary centres in the UK. Recruited patients did not have major structural brain malformations nor clinically significant copy number defects on microarray. Standardised clinical information was collected using a pre-test questionnaire completed by the recruiting clinician. Lymphocyte DNA was collected in all cases using standard procedures. We selected genes for analysis in the panel that were established causes of early-onset seizures and/or severe developmental delay in patients without frequent major structural brain anomalies. Genes leading to neurometabolic disorders with readily identifiable blood/urine/cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers were not included in the panel. The genes analysed were ADSL, ALG13, ARHGEF9, ARX, ATP1A3, ATRX, CDKL5, CHD2, CHRNA4, CHRNB2, CNTNAP2, EHMT1, FOXG1, GABRB3, GRIN2A, GRIN2B, KCNQ2, KCNT1, KIAA1279, LGI1, MAGI2, MBD5, MECP2, MEF2C, NRXN1, PCDH19, PIGA, PLCB1, PNKP, POLG, PRRT2, SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, SLC16A2, SLC25A22, SLC2A1, SLC9A6, SPTAN1, STXBP1, SYNGAP1, TBC1D24, TCF4, UBE2A, UBE3A and ZEB2 . We performed our analyses over 18 months in three phases, adding newly discovered genes to the panel as they were identified and employing improved sequence capture technology as it became available (see online S1). In phase 1, 48 patients were analysed through 29 genes. In phase 2, 94 patients were analysed through 39 genes. In phase 3, 258 patients were analysed through 46 genes (see online S1). Results We identified causative mutations in 71 patients (18%; see , online S1 and ). The most frequently mutated gene was SCN2A (11 patients, 3%), occurring de novo in all patients. Other recurrently mutated genes included CDKL5, KCNQ2 , SCN8A (six patients each), FOXG1, MECP2, SCN1A, STXBP1 (five patients each), KCNT1, PCDH19 , TCF4 (three patients each) and ATP1A3, PRRT2 and SCL9A6 (two patients each). Mutations in EHMT1, GABRB3, LGI1, MBD5, PIGA, UBE3A and ZEB2 were each found in single patients. Of the 54 patients for whom parental samples were available, 51 mutations were confirmed as de novo . For two patients, both harbouring KCNQ2 variants, mutations were inherited from a similarly affected parent. One FOXG1 variant had been inherited from the child's mother, who was mosaic for the mutation and clinically unaffected. Sixty-eight variants were either point mutations or small insertions and deletions. Three were larger de novo copy number abnormalities detected on our targeted array, a deletion encompassing MBD5 and two other genes (confirmed by FISH using probe RP11-548K3), a single-exon deletion within MECP2 and a multiexon duplication within CDKL5 (both confirmed by MLPA using kits P015-E1 and P189-B1, respectively). In a number of cases, electroclinical diagnoses considered strongly suggestive of the causative gene were only reached after re-examination of the phenotype in the light of the identified mutation. For example, we found a KCNT1 mutation in a child later recognised to have classical EIMFS (case 23) rather than the initial diagnosis of epileptic encephalopathy with multifocal EEG discharges. The cost of gene panel analysis in a diagnostic setting is now similar to that of Sanger sequencing a single gene. Therefore, while targeted single-gene Sanger sequencing may remain appropriate in some cases, for example, typical SCN1A -related phenotypes, EIMFS ( KCNT1 ), classical Rett syndrome ( MECP2 ) and some cases with other dysmorphic syndromes, our data argue for the use of panel-based analysis as the diagnostic genetic test of choice in the majority of individuals with early-onset seizure and severe developmental delay disorders. With time, we expect that panel analysis will evolve to use data generated from sequencing larger numbers of genes, for example, the whole exome or the clinical exome (all known disease genes). Potential advantages include the ability to add newly discovered genes without the need to redesign the assay and to analyse larger panels of genes without running a separate test. However, we currently find the better sequence coverage offered by a carefully designed and curated panel outweighs these potential benefits in a diagnostic setting. We note that the mutation detection rate we report in our early-onset seizure cases is similar to that reported in studies employing whole-exome sequencing in similar cohorts. While next-generation sequencing is a relatively new technology, in many respects it is equally as robust as Sanger sequencing. In some respects, it may be more robust, for example, in the detection of low-level mosaic mutations. We identified two mutations that had been missed despite previous Sanger sequencing of the gene in question. An SCN1A mutation (case 39) had been missed due to a technical interpretation error, less likely with more bioinformatics-driven interpretation pipelines used in the analysis of next-generation sequencing data. A MECP2 mutation (c.62+2_62+3delTG, in case 28) had also been missed because it affected the first exon of the gene, which many diagnostic laboratories have not sequenced until recently due to uncertainty about the most clinically relevant transcript. Like Sanger sequencing, next-generation sequencing remains poor at detecting exon-level copy number abnormalities, particularly when samples are run in the relatively small batches typical of a diagnostic setting. We, therefore, piloted the use of an exon-level microarray targeting our gene panel in a subset of our series. In our analysis of 33 cases without mutations on panel sequencing, we identified three likely pathogenic copy number abnormalities. Exon-level copy number analysis is also valuable in individuals harbouring single mutations in autosomal-recessive genes to search for second mutations and assist in the interpretation of the significance of sequence variants. Until next-generation sequencing allows robust copy number analysis, exon-level microarray will be a useful component of gene panel analysis and we have now integrated it into our standard analysis work stream. In conclusion, our work demonstrates the significant utility of a gene panel approach in the diagnosis of patients with early-onset epilepsy and severe developmental delay disorders, particularly the former. It also broadens the phenotypic spectrum, provides insights into the genotype–phenotype relationships of a number of the causative genes and emphasises the importance of exon-level copy number testing in their analysis.

Introduction Cerebral blood flow in small arteries is kept stable by the vasomotor response in healthy individuals, however, this protective mechanism may fail in elderly people or people suffering from cerebrovascular disease [ , ]. Emerging evidence suggests that blood flow dynamics diverge from average patterns in patients with vascular pathologies [ , ]. Patients with unilateral or bilateral extracranial carotid artery stenosis often exhibit hemodynamic abnormalities in the cerebral vasculature, including a reduced perfusion pressure when intracerebral collateral circulation is insufficient [ , ]. Previous studies have shown that patients with asymptomatic occlusion of the internal carotid artery (ICA) have a better preserved hemodynamic status of the brain compared with symptomatic patients with a stenosed carotid artery [ , , , ]. Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) is the recommended treatment for patients with symptomatic significant (> 50 %) carotid artery stenosis to restore cerebral blood flow and prevent future stroke [ ]. Carotid artery stenting (CAS) is an alternative for patients unsuitable for CEA and in younger patients [ ]. Hemodynamic disturbances contribute to approximately 50 % of perioperative strokes following CEA, playing a pivotal role in the diverse pathogenesis of postoperative stroke [ , ]. Cerebral hyper perfusion syndrome (CHS) is a relatively rare (0 – 3 %), potentially devastating complication leading to stroke [ , ]. Transcranial doppler (TCD) is the golden standard for monitoring intra-operative changes in the blood flow of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), thereby helping to reduce cerebral hyper perfusion related morbidity and mortality following CEA [ , ]. Advances in ultra-high field magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) comprising the 7 Tesla (7T) scanner, have enabled, precise, in vivo measurement of blood flow velocity (Vmean) and pulsatility index (PI) within the brain’s small perforating arteries, providing a valuable tool for assessing the cerebral microcirculation [ , ]. Prior research has shown that carotid occlusive disease may be associated with abnormal blood flow in cerebral perforating arteries across a broad patient cohort, including those with significant carotid artery stenosis not eligible for CEA, as well as those with an occlusion of the internal carotid artery (ICA) [ ]. While recent studies have compared flow abnormalities between these affected patients and the healthy population, no research to date has examined the hemodynamic impact of CEA on the relationship between pre- and postoperative cerebral blood flow dynamics and pulsatility in the small brain vessels [ , ]. This study aims to address the existing gap by utilizing 7T MRI 2D phase-contrast imaging to evaluate changes in blood flow velocity and pulsatility within the cerebral microcirculation in symptomatic patients with ipsilateral significant carotid artery stenosis undergoing CEA. Materials and methods Carotis7T study and study population The data used in this study originates from the Carotis7T Study, a monocentre prospective observational study at the University Medical Center Utrecht. Approval of the medical ethical committee (NedMec) has been obtained (NL 63,925.041.18) and the study has been conducted in accordance with the declaration of Helsinki [ ]. Patient recruitment took place between December 2021 and September 2024. All patients were discussed in a multidisciplinary team and CEA procedures were performed according to national and international guidelines [ ]. Included patients were compatible for MRI and had a symptomatic carotid artery stenosis of at least 50 % according to the North America Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial (NASCET) criteria [ ]. All included participants provided written informed consent, after which 3T and 7T brain MRI were performed one day prior to surgery and three months after surgery. Preoperative baseline measurements were used as control condition, allowing each patient to act as their own control. Symptomatic disease was defined as a transient ischemic attack (TIA), stroke or amaurosis fugax within 6 months prior to surgical intervention. Patients with contraindications for MRI, previous CEA or carotid artery stenting (CAS) in the artery to be treated, recent revascularization of the contralateral carotid artery, vertebral artery or intracranial artery carried out within 6 weeks prior to CEA, recent coronary artery bypass grafting within 3 months prior to inclusion or other major surgery within 6 weeks of inclusion were excluded.
