Discussion In this exploratory study, we measured cerebral blood flow velocity and pulsatility, measured at the levels of the MCA, BG and CSO, before and after CEA in patients with symptomatic carotid artery stenosis. The measured Vmean increased at the level of the M1, decreased at both the BG and CSO and the measured PI was higher at all levels. However, none of these changes were statistically significant. The observed values for BG and CSO perforating artery Vmean and PI in our patient population is of a similar magnitude compared to previous findings in elderly and patients with carotid artery stenosis. Across all participants, a gradual decline in both Vmean and PI was found from the MCA toward the CSO, indicating a reduction in blood flow parameters toward deeper brain structures [ , ] The observed nonsignificant increase in Vmean at the level of the MCA postoperatively, is in line with previous literature [ ]. Hemodynamic alterations at the MCA level lead to cerebral hyper perfusion in 13.2 % and cerebral hyper perfusion syndrome in 3.5 % of the patients undergoing CEA [ ]. The accompanying nonsignificant increase in PI is likely related to the decrease in inflow resistance, which reduces the amplitude of the reflection wave, after removal of the carotid stenosis [ , ]. This slight increase in PI was also observed at the levels of the perforating arteries, indicating that the hemodynamic effects of CEA may extend beyond large arteries and influence the cerebral microcirculation. In contrast, a decrease in Vmean was noted in these vessels, although this finding requires confirmation in a larger cohort. This opposite effect on the Vmean in the perforating arteries compared to the MCA may suggest that different autoregulatory mechanisms are at play in the microvasculature compared to larger cerebral arteries, possibly reflecting the presence of smooth muscle-mediated vasomotor regulation in larger arteries. If confirmed, the underlying mechanism remains uncertain and may be related to regional differences in vascular reactivity, autoregulatory adjustments, or metabolic demand [ ]. Interpretation of these hemodynamic parameters is challenging, as multiple vascular changes occur simultaneously following revascularization. Postoperatively, a decline in the number of perforating arteries is observed at both the BG and CSO levels [ , ]. Similar trends have been reported in other vascular systems, such as cardiac collaterals, where regression occurs during long-term follow-up [ , ]. Additionally, studies in Moyamoya patients have demonstrated a reduction in leptomeningeal collaterals following cerebral revascularization, accompanied by an increase in total hemispheric blood flow [ ]. Collateral development capacity is influenced by age, with older individuals exhibiting reduced collateral formation in large vessel occlusion. This age-related collateral rarefaction is characterized by a decline in collateral number and diameter, as well as increased vessel tortuosity [ , ]. The observation may also reflect generally larger diameters of perforating arteries before CEA, as autoregulatory vasodilation in response to carotid stenosis reduces vascular resistance and increases vessel caliber, thereby enhancing their detectability on MRI [ ]. Most included vessels are similar to or smaller than the voxel size, particularly in the BG and CSO regions where mean velocity is used as a threshold, making smaller diameters more prone to partial volume effects that reduce velocity readouts and lower detectability [ , ]. Although different vessels may be included pre- and postoperatively, consistent thresholding based on physiological properties across time points ensures that averaged values still reflect the overall hemodynamic state of this category of vessels. Future studies could optimize acquisition and co-registration methods to enable repeated detection of the same vessels, allowing more detailed assessment of microvascular adaptation after CEA. Gray matter CBF was comparable to those of age-matched populations and showed no significant postoperative change [ ]. This suggests that, despite regression of collaterals and alterations in perforating artery morphology, cortical perfusion is preserved, likely reflecting compensatory autoregulatory mechanisms at the tissue level. A possible explanation for this discrepancy may be attributed to the inclusion of patients with carotid occlusion within the latter cohort, whereas carotid occlusion served as an exclusion criterium and is therefore absent in our study population. In individuals with complete carotid occlusion and an anatomically intact circle of Willis or sufficient collaterals, the contralateral ICA can compensate by supplying blood to the affected hemisphere, possibly explaining the lower Vmean and PI [ ]. Given that hemodynamic disturbances, characterized as intra- or postprocedural bradycardia, asystole or any hypotension requiring treatment, account for nearly 50 % of ischemic strokes in a large Dutch cohort with recently symptomatic carotid artery stenosis, early detection and prevention is of critical importance [ ]. In the context of our small cohort, our findings did not reach statistical significance, but they may reflect early adaptive responses in cerebral hemodynamics. Our study has certain limitations. First, the small penetrating arteries analysed in this study are close to the detection limits of 7T MRI. Most of the included vessels have diameters comparable to or smaller than the voxel size, making them particularly susceptible to partial volume effects. These effects typically result in an overestimation of the PI and an underestimation of Vmean, possibly contributing partly to the observed (non-significant) decrease post-operatively [ ]. However, these effects are present in both the pre-and postoperative images, which allows at least to observe relative changes. Second, few scans were excluded due to poor image quality resulting from subject movement during scanning (BG: 6.7 % preoperatively, 13.3 % postoperatively and CSO: 13.3 % preoperatively and 26.7 % postoperatively). Additionally, motion may have affected the included scans, potentially reducing their quality. This limitation was also reported in other studies and can be explained by our relatively older population with a higher tendency to move during MRI scanning than younger people [ , ]. Various strategies can be employed to reduce motion effects, including acquisitions that track and correct motion or techniques that monitor motion during scanning, which can then be statistically controlled during analysis [ ]. Third, methodological variations may have influenced the results. Although the planning followed a predefined protocol, some degrees of freedom remained unavoidable. This could affect the pre- and postoperative planning and associated variability in the measured values, since planning was performed manually by multiple experience operators (JZ, EV, EH). Lastly, our study was limited by a relatively small sample size of fifteen patients. The imaging protocol, which included a 30-minute 3T MRI scan followed by a 60 – 75-minute 7T MRI scan, along with the fact that patients recently experienced a stroke within 14 days of undergoing CEA, likely contributed to a high rate of participant opt-out (58 %). Future studies could focus on selecting only the most essential 7T sequences, improving patient preparation and comfort, with features such as better table padding or audiovisual distraction to make participation more tolerable, especially in patients with recent brain infarction. The aforementioned limitations, combined with the inevitable limited signal-to-noise ratio in these small vessels, may have prevented us from observing any differences in Vmean or the PI at the level of the MCA, BG and CSO in our study. Conclusion In our cohort of patients with symptomatic carotid artery stenosis undergoing CEA, we observed no significant changes in Vmean and PI at the level of the M1, BG and CSO. These findings suggest that, in this small sample, surgical removal of carotid stenosis did not result in a measurable impact on brain perforating artery flow at all levels. However, subtle trends were noted, and in a larger cohort, these hemodynamic parameters may provide more definitive insights into the cerebrovascular effects of carotid revascularization and the underlying pathophysiology of carotid artery disease. Brief overview in historical context In 1498, Jakob Sprenger and Heinrich Kraemer published “Maleus maleficarum” (hammer of witches) and described a priest with motor and vocal tics, thought to be caused by demonic influence. In 1825, Jean Marc Gaspard Itard described “the case of a cussing Marquise,” (with) premonitory sensation, echolalia and coprolalia. Gilles de la Tourette in 1895 described 9 patients who suffered from a disorder characterized by involuntary movements, echolalia, echopraxia, coprolalia, and strange, uncontrollable sounds [ ]. Tourette surmised this was a “degenerative disorder of the nervous system, which was partially due to the immoral behaviors of previous generations”Later, Charcot (Tourette’s mentor) would rename this disorder Tourette syndrome [ ]. Characteristics and course Historically, Tourette syndrome (TS) has primarily been considered a disorder of childhood. The Tourette International Consortium reported a mean age of onset of 6.4 years in 6805 patients with TS with a mean age at diagnosis of 13.2 years, demonstrating a 7-year gap before diagnosis was made. They noted a 4.4:1 male to female predominance. Associated comorbidities included attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in 55.6%, obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) in 54.9%, anger issues (27.6%), learning problems (22%), mood disorders (16.9%), anxiety (16%), conduct disorder (12.3%), and pervasive developmental disorder (4.6%). A positive family history of tic disorder was present in 51.7% [ ]. The Danish National Tourette Clinic reported on 314 patients with age ranging from 5 to 19 years with a diagnosis of TS. They noted that tic severity commonly tended to decline gradually during adolescence. After the age of 16 years, tic resolution had occurred in 17.7%, mild residual tics persisted in 59.5% and moderate to severe tics continued in 22.8%. There was a strong tendency for neuropsychiatric comorbidities to persist (63%). They concluded that the “severity of tics, OCD, and ADHD were significantly associated with age and declined during adolescence; however, considerable comorbidities and coexisting psychopathologies tended to persist through later adolescence” [ ]. The European Clinical Guidelines for Tourette Syndrome indicated 80% of individuals who present with tics at under age 10 experienced a significant decrease in tic frequency and severity during adolescence by the age of 18 years will most commonly no longer experience impairment from tics; however, tics persisted in 20%, and in some circumstances worsened and became debilitating [ ]. Tourette spectrum Our understanding of TS is rapidly changing. “The perception of TS as a rare, bizarre psychological disorder began to change in the 1960s”, and is now “recognized as a relatively common, biological, genetic disorder with a spectrum of neurobehavioral manifestations that wax and wane during over time during its natural course. The marked fluctuations in the severity and frequency of symptoms, coupled with the striking variation in manifestations from one patient to another, however, contribute to frequent misdiagnosis” (Jankovic, 2001) Many medical providers primarily consider TS to be a tic disorder that often includes neuropsychiatric comorbidities, and place their treatment emphasis on minimizing tics; however, TS is a clinical spectrum and the therapeutic approach should be more comprehensive. The relationship between neuropsychiatric symptoms and tics is complex and intertwined. Each child or individual presents as a unique case within the spectrum. Jankovic stated that “because of the broad range of neurological and behavioral manifestations and their varying severity, therapy for TS must be individualized and tailored specifically to the needs of the patient, and the most troublesome symptoms should be targeted first.” (Jankovic, 2001) Hartmann added, “personalized treatments in Tourette syndrome are both necessary because of the width of the clinical spectrum, making every patient unique from a symptom-oriented perspective; yet, difficult to achieve because of the lack of large prospective cohorts which may inform on prognostic factors and disease-modifying interventions.” (Hartman) When considering the potential neuropsychiatric disorders within the Tourette spectrum, all diagnostic criteria may not be met for a given disorder independently, but associated clinical characteristics may be present to some degree. A child might not meet all diagnostic criteria for ADHD, yet still have varying degrees of hyperactivity or problems with attention/focus. Similarly, a child might not meet diagnostic criteria for generalized anxiety disorder, yet still show signs of excessive worrying. The diagnostic criteria for OCD might not be met, yet the individual may obsess over certain routines or feel compelled to perform rituals to avoid something bad from happening. Stern said, “less intrusive obsessionality is clearly very common, and represents obsessive-compulsive behavior. Tourettic obsessionality is clinically distinct from pure obsessive-compulsive disorder” [ ]. Assessment for signs and symptoms of common neuropsychiatric problems will allow the treatment team to comprehend the complexity of each child in order to create an optimal individualized therapy plan. General considerations for treatment Once education has been achieved, the discussion can move to the therapeutic approach and treatment options. The first determination is if tic severity warrants treatment. Are the tics bothering the child and causing a negative impact or dysfunction? Often, especially with younger children, the child may not even be aware of the tics. The tics may bother the parent, but not the child. Essentially, if negative impact on the child is absent or minimal, medication is not warranted. Medical therapy should be considered when the tics negatively impact the child’s self-esteem or ability to function, or if tics produce discomfort or pain. If medical therapy is considered, it is critical to establish appropriate expectations, and ensure that patients and families understand it is rare for treatment to result in complete tic resolution. On average, medications for tics can reduce symptoms by about 25–50% [ ]. The goal should be reasonable tic control and reduction of associated impairment, to maximize the child’s quality of life and ability to function [ ]. The treatment plan should be developed with consideration of the potential need to also treat neuropsychiatric morbidities, and to avoid treatment options that may adversely impact comorbidities. Treatment for Tourette spectrum with ADHD, Tics dominant Central α<sub>2</sub> adrenergic agonists Clonidine and guanfacine are central α 2 adrenergic agonists used to treat ADHD and tics when they occur in combination. These medications can be given alone or in combination with a stimulant if ADHD symptoms are prominent. Clonidine is often prescribed as a first line treatment for tic prevention, and may also have a positive impact on inattention and hyperactivity with a relatively low side effect profile. Formulations include immediate release tablets and an extended release transdermal patch. In prior studies, the most significant improvement occurred in response to combination therapy [ ]. The clonidine transdermal patch was evaluated as therapy in a randomized double blind, multicenter, placebo-controlled trial for the treatment of tic disorders conducted in China. There were 437 patients, diagnosed with either transient tic disorder (5%), chronic tic disorder (40%), or Tourette syndrome (55%). The tic severity score decreased by 69% in response to clonidine patch, but also decreased by 47% in the placebo group [ ]. The recommended starting dose is 0.05 mg per day. The dose should be titrated slowly to effect to a total dose of 0.1–0.3 mg per day in adults and children, divided 3–4 times per day. Hypotension and bradycardia can occur and blood pressure and heart rate should be monitored [ ]. Guanfacine is supplied as immediate and sustained release tablets. In a randomized, double blind, 8-week trial in a group of 34 subjects with ADHD combined type and tic disorder, guanfacine reduced tic severity by 31% compared to no significant change in the placebo group. The authors concluded that guanfacine was “safe and effective in short term treatment of ADHD and tic disorder, and a combination of these medications might allow lower doses of stimulant” [ ]. It is important to monitor for possible QTc prolongation when treating with guanfacine, especially when the patient has a history of cardiac condition, is taking other medications that might lengthen QTc, or has a positive family history of QTc prolongation. The recommended starting dose is 0.5 mg per day and can be titrated to up to 4 mg per day [ ].
